cover.title: Outside four immigration-related units, backlog has risen in stages
cover.body: Outside USCIS, CBP, ICE and EOIR, year-end backlog relative to annual receipts climbed from about 10% in FY2011–13 to 26.0% in FY2020–25. The FY2020–25 average is 9.1 points above FY2014–19, and at least 8.0 after removing any single unit. 69 of 96 agencies rose.
cover.foot: Year-end backlog (Table 26) ÷ requests received that year (Table 01). Dotted lines: period averages. The government-wide ratio (dashed) rose only about 3 points.

steps.title: Backlog counts rise, but the ratio goes up and down

p: Backlog is requests still open at year end past the legal deadline (Table 26). The ratio sets that year-end stock beside the year's receipts; it is not the chance that a request became backlogged.

The government-wide backlog count rises overall (339,756 in FY2025), but backlog ÷ receipts goes up and down. A unit with very large receipts weighs heavily in the denominator, so the next step separates units.

steps.method: Backlog: Table 26. Receipts: requests received, Table 01.

steps.title: Why the government-wide ratio barely moves

p: The four units (USCIS, CBP, ICE and EOIR) receive a growing share of requests: 19.7% in FY2008, 47.3% in FY2019 and 56.4% in FY2025. Their backlog follows a different path.
Six-year averages: all agencies 15.7% to 18.8% (+3.1 points); the four units 14.2% to 12.8% (−1.4); outside the four units 16.9% to 26.0% (+9.1).

sections.h: Why the total rose only about 3 points
p: Outside the four units the ratio rose 9.08 points, but those units hold only 50.1% of receipts, so they add +4.55; the four units' own ratio fell slightly (−0.39); their growing share of receipts pulled the total down by 0.92; total +3.24 (table). From here on, look outside the four units.

steps.method: Six-year totals of backlog and receipts are divided for the split, so it differs slightly from the yearly averages.

steps.title: A rise in stages since FY2013, steepest in FY2020

p: Backlog ÷ receipts outside the four units, with each period's average (dotted lines), and a second line without DOS, which added the most backlog.

Averages: 13.5% in FY2008–10, 10.1% in FY2011–13, 16.9% in FY2014–19 and 26.0% in FY2020–25. It climbed in stages, with five down years out of twelve; the largest single-year rises are FY2020 (+8.9), FY2025 (+8.0) and FY2014 (+4.7).
From FY2013 to FY2019 it had already risen 8.2 points, so FY2020 is not presented as a break. Without DOS the ratio still rises from 16.5% in FY2019 to 24.5% in FY2020 and stays higher.
27 agencies have receipts in FY2010 but none in FY2008, so the rise is safer to state from FY2011–13.

charts.title: Backlog ÷ receipts outside the four units

steps.title: Broad: 69 of 96 agencies rose, mainly within agencies

p: The 96 agencies with data in every year FY2014–25 (99.8% of FY2020–25 receipts outside the four units); six-year totals of backlog and receipts, FY2014–19 against FY2020–25.
69 of 96 agencies rose (72%), 24 of the 28 with at least 6,000 receipts in each window (86%). Split by agency, the within-agency change is +9.20 on average of the +9.03 total.

The large traditional departments all rose: DoW (DoD) 18.2% to 34.4%, DOJ (excluding EOIR) 29.8% to 49.9%, HHS 15.9% to 27.7%, DOT 19.9% to 37.6%, DOS 90.4% to 116.2%. DOS's backlog now exceeds a year of its receipts.
Three large ones fell: DHS's other components (a mix effect from PRIV and CISA), VA (mainly VBA: 36.9% to 3.1%) and EEOC.

steps.method: Hollow dot: FY2014–19; filled dot: FY2020–25. DHS and DOJ here exclude the four units.

steps.title: The FY2020 jump and the FY2023–24 dip come from a few units' receipts

p: Receipts fell from 452,915 to 375,203 (−17.2%) while backlog rose from 84,549 to 103,458 (+22.4%). Of the 77,712 drop in receipts, NARA accounts for 41,728 and DHS PRIV for 18,903, 78% together; the rise in backlog is spread out (DHS's other components +4,247, DoW (DoD) +2,802, DOS +2,692, DOJ +2,607).

VBA and PRIV received many more requests while carrying little backlog, which enlarged the denominator. Without these two units the ratio is 27.6% or higher in every year from FY2020, with no dip; the FY2020–25 average is 14.1 points above FY2014–19.
The main population does not change: choosing units to remove after seeing the results would be choosing data for the conclusion. In this check the gap is larger than the 9.1 points, not smaller.

steps.method: Same ratio, with units whose receipts swing sharply left out.

charts.title: Backlog ÷ receipts, removing units with large swings in receipts

steps.title: A second measure moves the same way

p: Requests pending at year end (Table 01) count every open request regardless of the deadline, so they avoid differences in how agencies apply deadlines.

Pending at year end ÷ receipts moves the same way: 15.0% in FY2013, 25.1% in FY2019, 35.1% in FY2020 and 37.8% in FY2025. Backlog as a share of pending stays between 69.4% and 81.2% in all 18 years: the rise shows in both measures, not only in backlog. The reports cannot show whether agencies changed how they count.

On a denominator of perfected requests only, the increase is larger: 18.2% to 30.0%, 11.8 points. On this denominator the gap is larger than the 9.1 points: a check of the choice of denominator, not proof of a lower bound.

steps.method: Perfected requests processed: Tables 16–18. Only perfected requests can be backlogged.

charts.title: Outside the four units: four ratios

steps.title: 9.1 points higher, at least 8.0 after removing any single unit

p: The FY2020–25 average is 9.1 points above FY2014–19 (16.9% to 26.0%, about 1.5 times). After removing any single unit (590 removals) it is at least 8.0; without FY2025 it is 8.3, and at least 7.0.
“Every year from FY2020 is above every earlier year” has a margin of only 0.8 points at its tightest (removing NARA), so the finding uses the average difference instead.

sections.h: When the following year's report differs
p: The next year's report repeats the prior year's backlog and receipts; by rule they should be identical. Seven matched backlog figures differ by 500 or more. Using them instead, the gap is 10.01 (backlog replaced) or 9.82 (backlog and receipts replaced): slightly larger. In three cases the replacement equals the unit's pending requests at the start of the next year, so these are only a reference.

steps.method: One unit removed at a time, from all years; agencies without components count once.

charts.title: Backlog ÷ receipts outside the four units, with following-year figures

steps.title: Almost half of the FY2025 backlog is at three units

p: Government-wide backlog in FY2025 is 339,756: CBP 96,303 (28.3%), PRIV 48,433 (14.3%) and DOS Main 22,678 (6.7%), together 49.3%. Outside the four units holds 65.6% of the backlog and 43.6% of receipts.

sections.h: Why the four units are not the main story
p: Their own ratio swings widely (65.7% in FY2008, 8.8% in FY2019). CBP's backlog went from 21,444 in FY2023 to 110,271 in FY2024; USCIS's from 20,344 in FY2020 to 1,599 in FY2021.
Backlog outside the four units rose by 87,290 in one year, 44,359 of it at PRIV; FY2025 has no following-year report to check against yet.

steps.title: Outside four immigration-related units, backlog has risen in stages

p: Outside USCIS, CBP, ICE and EOIR, year-end backlog relative to annual receipts climbed from about 10% in FY2011–13 to 26.0% in FY2020–25; the FY2020–25 average is 9.1 points above FY2014–19, and at least 8.0 after removing any single unit. The rise is mainly within agencies and broad. The government-wide ratio rose only about 3 points because the four units have low ratios and a growing share of receipts.
That backlog pressure is flat government-wide, without the split.
That FY2020 was a break caused by a single event: the ratio had already risen 8.2 points from FY2013 to FY2019.
That the lower FY2023–24 values mean relief: they reflect larger receipts at VBA and PRIV.
That this population is “non-immigration requests”: it is a grouping of units, not of request topics.
DOS: 90.4% to 116.2%, more than a year of receipts · DOJ (excluding EOIR): 29.8% to 49.9% · PRIV's FY2025 backlog, 4,074 to 48,433.

steps.method: Annual totals reported by the agencies themselves; the reports do not show causes. Full analysis: Storyline 4 notebook.
